summary: Discovery of Designated Resolvers (DDR) lets a client that only knows a resolver's IP address find that resolver's encrypted DNS settings using DNS records. It can move a client from unencrypted DNS to encrypted DNS. It is intended only for cases where the unencrypted resolver and its designated resolver are run by the same or cooperating entities.

eli5.summary: You know a helper by their street address only. DDR is a way to ask them "do you have a private door?" and then use it, if the same person runs it.

questions: discover doh endpoint from resolver ip
how does a client discover encrypted dns
subtitle: How a device that only knows a DNS server's IP address can find out whether that server offers encrypted DNS, and verify it.

tldr.problem: Networks usually hand out only the IP address of a DNS resolver, but encrypted DNS (DoT, DoQ, DoH) can need a hostname, other addresses, a non-standard port or a URI Template.
tldr.mechanism: The client asks the resolver for SVCB records at the special name _dns.resolver.arpa, or at _dns plus the resolver name when it knows the resolver's name. It then checks the TLS certificate before switching to the Designated Resolver it learned about.
tldr.outcome: A client can move from unencrypted to encrypted DNS automatically, but only to a resolver run by the same or a cooperating entity. On-path attackers can still block discovery.

today: RFC 9462 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2023. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata. Its companion RFC 9463 defines DHCP and Router Advertisement options, which take precedence over DDR when both are present.

sections.title: The Problem and the Two Mechanisms
sections.content:
Clients that want to use encrypted DNS such as DNS over TLS (DoT), DNS over QUIC (DoQ) or DNS over HTTPS (DoH) can need more than an IP address. They may need the resolver's hostname, alternate IP addresses, non-standard ports or URI Templates. Common configuration mechanisms, such as DHCP, IPv6 Router Advertisement options and manual configuration, usually provide only the resolver's IP address.

RFC 9462 defines Discovery of Designated Resolvers (DDR) with two mechanisms, both built on DNS Service Binding (SVCB) records from RFC 9460. When only the IP address of an Unencrypted DNS Resolver is known, the client queries a special-use domain name. When the hostname of an Encrypted DNS Resolver is known, the client sends an SVCB query for that name.

"Designated" means the resolvers are operated by the same entity or cooperating entities. For example, they are reachable on the same IP address, or a certificate contains the IP address of the original resolver.
sections.eli5: Usually you are given just a house number for a helper. DDR is a way to ask the house for its other doors and phone numbers, and to make sure they belong to the same family.

sections.title: Terms and SVCB Records
sections.content:
A Designated Resolver is a resolver, presumably an Encrypted DNS Resolver, designated by another resolver for use in its own place. An Unencrypted DNS Resolver uses a transport without encryption, historically TCP or UDP port 53.

Designated Resolvers are described by ServiceMode SVCB records for DNS servers. AliasMode records can point clients at the right ServiceMode record. The record format, including DNS-specific parameters such as dohpath, is defined in RFC 9461. Resolvers can express a preference among several records with the SVCB priority field.

If a client sees a mandatory parameter it does not understand, it MUST NOT use that record, but it can still use other records in the same response. A client that supports only DoH and DoT can therefore skip a record for a protocol that does not exist yet.

To avoid name lookup deadlock, a client must not use a given Encrypted DNS Resolver for the queries needed to resolve that resolver's own name or to check its certificate revocation status.
sections.eli5: Each record is like a business card that says which kind of private line to use and where. If a card uses a language you cannot read, you skip it and read the next card.

sections.title: Discovery Using a Resolver IP Address
sections.content:
When a client is configured with an Unencrypted DNS Resolver IP address, it SHOULD query that resolver for SVCB records of a service with scheme dns and authority resolver.arpa before making other queries. Concretely, it asks for _dns.resolver.arpa. with the SVCB record type (64).

ServiceMode answers MUST NOT use . or resolver.arpa as the TargetName, and clients MUST NOT perform A or AAAA queries for resolver.arpa. The resolver SHOULD put the A and AAAA records for the Designated Resolver's name in the Additional section, saving the client a round trip. A Designated Resolver SHOULD be reachable over the address families its unencrypted counterpart supports, and SHOULD NOT support fewer. If a resolver has no Designated Resolver, it SHOULD return NODATA.

A client MUST NOT reuse a designation found through one resolver's IP address for any other resolver, and it SHOULD NOT reuse one across different networks without repeating discovery, since the same IP address may be a different server elsewhere.
sections.eli5: You send a special question to the helper you already know: "Who are your private helpers?" The answer is a list of names and doors. A list you got from one helper only counts for that helper.

sections.title: Verified and Opportunistic Discovery
sections.content:
A client MUST NOT automatically use a Designated Resolver without validation. The RFC defines two ways to do it. Verified Discovery uses a TLS certificate. The client MUST verify the certificate chain to a trust anchor under RFC 5280, and MUST verify that the certificate contains the IP address of the designating Unencrypted DNS Resolver in an iPAddress entry of the subjectAltName extension.

If the checks pass, the client SHOULD use the Designated Resolver wherever it would have used the unencrypted one. If they fail, the client MUST NOT automatically use it when the designation was found only through a _dns.resolver.arpa. query. It SHOULD also stop asking for the length of the record's TTL. The IP address used for the connection may differ from the original, but the certificate checks still apply to the original address.

Opportunistic Discovery is for resolvers on private IP addresses, Unique Local Addresses and Link-Local addresses, whose identity cannot usually be confirmed by a certificate. A client MAY use the SVCB information with the opportunistic privacy profile as long as the Encrypted DNS Resolver has the same IP address as the Unencrypted one. Clients SHOULD use this mode only for private or local addresses.
sections.eli5: Before using a new private door, you check an ID card that lists the street address you started from. If you are inside a gated neighbourhood where nobody can show such a card, you only trust a door at exactly the same address.

sections.title: Discovery Using a Resolver Name
sections.content:
A client that already knows the name of an Encrypted DNS Resolver, from configuration or from a provisioning protocol such as DNR (RFC 9463), sends an SVCB query for _dns. plus that name. The query can go to the named resolver or to any other resolver. These records SHOULD be in the public DNS if the name's A or AAAA records are.

In the RFC's example, a client that knows a DoT server resolver.example.com asks for _dns.resolver.example.com and learns that the name supports DoH at priority 1 and DoT at priority 2.

The client MUST check that the resolver's certificate contains the known name in a subjectAltName extension, even when the SVCB TargetName is a different name. This validation is unrelated to whichever resolver supplied the SVCB answer. The RFC notes this is useful when a client has a DoT configuration but sits on a network that blocks DoT, since it can ask another accessible resolver whether a DoH server exists.
sections.eli5: If you already know a helper's name, you can ask anyone, "What other ways can I reach this helper?" Then you check that the person who answers the door really has that name.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
A DNS forwarder SHOULD NOT forward queries for resolver.arpa upstream, because the client would get a record that fails authentication when the forwarder's IP address is not in the upstream certificate. A completely transparent forwarder MAY forward them in specific cases. Resolvers that support DDR MUST treat resolver.arpa as a locally served zone per RFC 6303, answering NODATA for any query type other than SVCB at _dns.resolver.arpa..

Resolver owners supporting Verified Discovery need to list the valid referring IP addresses in their certificates, which may be hard with many addresses. Clients MUST NOT use resolver.arpa as the TLS SNI or as the DoH URI host, and MUST use the original resolver IP as the DoH URI host. Since SNI does not support IP addresses by default, resolvers must present the right certificate when no SNI is sent.

If the network provides DNR information over DHCP or Router Advertisements, clients can skip the resolver.arpa query for that resolver, and DNR SHOULD take precedence in a conflict because it is considered more reliable.
sections.eli5: Helpers who pass questions along must not pass this one on, or the answer would come from the wrong place. And if the network already gave you a card listing the private doors, trust the card first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SVCB answers may arrive over unencrypted DNS, so an on-path attacker can drop queries or answers and stop a client from switching to encrypted DNS. A client may not be able to tell that from a resolver that has no Designated Resolver, so it can re-send its queries periodically. Attackers who block connections to the encrypted server can also prevent the switch.

Encrypted DNS Resolvers MUST NOT behave differently based solely on SVCB metadata such as the HTTP path or alternate port, because an attacker could change it. For example, an attacker could alter dohpath to pick an unfiltered service. The RFC suggests separate IP addresses or hostnames instead.

An attacker could try to steer traffic to an unrelated resolver with a valid certificate. For that reason Verified Discovery requires the unencrypted resolver's IP address to be covered by the certificate's SAN, and Opportunistic Discovery is limited to the same IP address. Appendix B explains why SVCB records were chosen: they keep client DNS logic self-contained, are extensible, and pair with TLS Encrypted ClientHello.
sections.eli5: A sneaky person can hide the note that points to the private door, so you stay on the open line. Your check of the ID card stops a fake door from fooling you.

sections.title: The resolver.arpa Name
sections.content:
IANA has registered resolver.arpa in the Special-Use Domain Names registry established by RFC 6761, and added it to the Transport-Independent Locally-Served DNS Zone Registry as "DNS Resolver Special-Use Domain".

Per the RFC, humans and applications do not need to treat the name specially, but DNS client libraries should use it to ask about a resolver's properties, and caching servers should not forward queries for it. Authoritative servers need no special handling. Appendix A compares it to ipv4only.arpa, where the client is not interested in an answer from the authoritative arpa servers, only from the resolver it is talking to.
sections.eli5: It is a made-up address that always means "ask the helper you are talking to about itself", never a real place on the internet.
